tips.title: Excess, filter, crystallise
tips.body: Three words in order carry most of the method. Add the solid **in excess** so all the acid is used; **filter** to remove what did not dissolve; **crystallise** the solution to get the solid salt. A method missing any one of the three loses a mark.

tips.title: Excess solid is the point, not a mistake
tips.body: Adding **more solid than can react** is deliberate. It guarantees **no acid is left**, which is what makes the product **pure** — and the leftover is easy to remove by **filtering**, whereas leftover acid is not.

tips.title: How you know the acid has gone
tips.body: The signal is that **solid stops disappearing** — it simply sits at the bottom. With a carbonate you can also say the **fizzing stops**. Either observation answers *how do you know all the acid has reacted?*

tips.title: Warm the acid, do not boil the solution
tips.body: A **Bunsen burner** gently warms the **acid** to speed the reaction up. The **solution** is then evaporated with a **water bath or electric heater**, not a flame — boiling it dry gives small, spoiled crystals and risks spitting.

tips.title: Slower evaporation, better crystals
tips.body: Evaporate to the point of crystallisation, then **leave the rest to evaporate slowly**. Large, well-formed crystals need time; driving all the water off quickly gives a powder.

why.matters:
A reaction that works is not the same thing as a method that gives a **pure** product, and this practical is about the difference. Acid and alkali neutralise perfectly well — but you cannot see when to stop, and whatever is left over is dissolved and cannot be got out again.

Swapping in an insoluble solid solves both problems at once: the endpoint becomes visible, and the excess can be filtered off. What is being taught here is the **design of an experiment**, which is a different skill from the chemistry inside it.

examples.title: Making Epsom salts out of a rock
examples.body:
Magnesium sulfate is sold for bath water and for garden soil, and it is made from magnesium oxide, a powder that will not dissolve in water at all. Add magnesium oxide to warm sulfuric acid until no more disappears, filter off what is left, and crystallise what comes through.

Three stages — **excess, filter, crystallise** — and each one is answering a question. Excess guarantees no acid survives. Filtering removes the only thing left that could contaminate the product. Crystallising turns a solution into something you can weigh.

visual.alt: A flow chart of the salt preparation: warm the acid, add the insoluble oxide a spatula at a time until solid stops disappearing, filter off the excess, then evaporate and leave the solution to crystallise into pure dry magnesium sulfate

examples.title: Why the chemist adds too much on purpose
examples.body:
Adding more solid than can possibly react looks like carelessness and is the whole design. The alternative is to stop at exactly the right moment, and with a dissolved alkali there is nothing to see: the solution looks the same one drop before the endpoint and one drop after.

An insoluble solid changes both halves of that. The endpoint is visible, because solid stops disappearing and sits at the bottom. And the leftover is **solid**, so a filter paper removes it — which nothing can do for leftover acid.

visual.alt: A table contrasting neutralising with a dissolved alkali, where the endpoint is invisible and any excess stays dissolved and cannot be removed, with using an insoluble solid, where the solid stops disappearing and the excess is filtered off

examples.title: Why big crystals take their time
examples.body:
Evaporate a salt solution over a flame and you get a spoiled powder. Leave the same solution on a windowsill for a week and you get crystals with flat faces and sharp edges, big enough to pick up.

Crystals grow by ions arriving at a surface and finding their place in the lattice. Given time, each one settles into the pattern; rushed, they pile up wherever they land. Every large crystal anyone has ever seen was slow — which is why a cave grows better crystals than a laboratory ever will.

steps.title: Why an insoluble solid is the right starting material
steps.body:
**Soluble salts can be made from acids by reacting them with solid insoluble substances**, such as metals, metal oxides, hydroxides or carbonates.

**This is required practical 1**, and the whole method is built around one problem: how do you know when to stop adding?

**The problem with an alkali.** If you neutralised the acid with a **solution** — sodium hydroxide, say — you could not see when you had added exactly enough. Too little and **acid is left**; too much and **alkali is left**. Either way the product is contaminated, and neither can be filtered out because both are dissolved.

**The solution is an insoluble solid.** Add it **in excess** — more than can possibly react. All the **acid** is used up, which is the point, and the **leftover solid does not dissolve**, so it can simply be **filtered off**.

**That is why the reactant must be insoluble.** It turns an invisible endpoint into a visible one, and it turns the excess from a problem into something you can remove with a filter funnel.

**The salt you get** follows the usual naming rule: the **acid** gives the ending and the **metal** gives the first word. Copper(II) oxide with sulfuric acid gives **copper(II) sulfate**.

steps.title: The details that carry marks
steps.body:
**Four choices in this practical are made for reasons**, and questions ask for the reasons rather than the steps.

**Why warm the acid.** To make the reaction **faster**. It is a rate question hiding in a preparation: warming gives the particles more energy, so they collide more often and more energetically.

**Why a water bath rather than a Bunsen flame for the evaporation.** A flame heats unevenly and can take the solution past dryness, which **spoils the crystals** and makes the mixture **spit**. A water bath cannot exceed 100 °C.

**Why not evaporate to dryness.** Driving off all the water gives a **powder** rather than crystals, and can **decompose** some salts. Stop when crystals **begin** to form, then let the rest go slowly.

**Why slow evaporation gives better crystals.** The particles have time to arrange themselves into a regular lattice. Fast evaporation traps them where they land, giving many small crystals instead of a few large ones.

**How you know the acid has all reacted.** The solid **stops disappearing** and collects at the bottom. If the solid is a **carbonate**, the **fizzing also stops**, which is a second observation you can give.

**A safety point worth having:** dilute acids are **irritants**, so **eye protection** is worn throughout, and hot apparatus is moved with **tongs**.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**The excess is the whole design of the experiment.** With a soluble alkali you cannot see the endpoint, and anything left over — acid or alkali — is **dissolved** and cannot be filtered out. Using an **insoluble** solid changes both problems at once: the endpoint becomes **visible** (solid stops disappearing) and the leftover becomes **removable** (filter it). An answer that says *so all the acid reacts* has half of it; adding *and the excess can be filtered off, which an excess of alkali could not be* has all of it.

**Every step has a reason, and the reasons are the marks.** *Warm the acid* is a **rate** decision. *Water bath* is about **even heating and not passing 100 °C**. *Stop when crystals start* avoids **powder and decomposition**. *Evaporate slowly* gives the particles time to form a **regular lattice**, so the crystals are larger.

**Pure and dry are two separate requirements.** **Purity** comes from the **excess plus filtration** — no acid left, no undissolved solid left. **Dryness** comes from the final step, patting between **filter paper** or leaving in a warm place. A question asking for *pure, dry crystals* is asking you to account for both words.

**The observation depends on the solid.** With an **oxide or hydroxide**, the signal is that the solid **stops dissolving**. With a **carbonate**, the **fizzing stops** as well, because carbon dioxide is no longer being produced. Giving the observation that matches the solid you were given shows you are reading the question rather than reciting the method.

**And the salt is predictable.** As always, the **acid** gives the ending and the **metal** gives the first word, so a preparation using an unfamiliar oxide is still a question you can answer completely.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would prepare a pure, dry sample of copper(II) sulfate crystals from copper(II) oxide and dilute sulfuric acid, giving a reason for each stage.
questions.solution:
I would measure dilute **sulfuric acid** into a beaker and **warm it gently** with a Bunsen burner. Warming is a **rate** decision: the particles gain energy, collide more often and more energetically, and the reaction goes faster.

I would then add **copper(II) oxide** a little at a time, stirring, until **no more dissolves** and solid begins to collect at the bottom. That solid is the **excess**, and adding it deliberately is the heart of the method: it guarantees that **all the acid has been used up**, so no acid can contaminate the product. It is also the signal that tells me to stop — with an insoluble solid the endpoint is **visible**, which it would not be if I neutralised the acid with a hydroxide **solution**.

Next I would **filter** the mixture. The unreacted copper(II) oxide is **insoluble**, so it stays in the filter paper, while the blue **copper(II) sulfate solution** passes through. This is the second reason for choosing an insoluble reactant: an excess of **alkali solution** would be dissolved and would pass straight through the filter with the salt.

I would pour the **filtrate** into an evaporating basin and heat it over a **water bath** rather than a flame — a water bath heats evenly and cannot exceed 100 °C, so the solution does not **spit** or pass dryness. I would stop heating as soon as **crystals began to form**. Evaporating to dryness would give a **powder** rather than crystals, and can decompose some salts.

Finally I would leave the remaining solution to **evaporate slowly** at room temperature. Slow evaporation gives the particles time to arrange into a **regular lattice**, so the crystals grow **larger and better formed**. Once dry I would **pat the crystals between filter paper**.

That gives crystals that are both **pure** — the excess and the filtration between them leave neither acid nor undissolved solid — and **dry**, which is the separate job of the last step.

questions.prompt: Explain why this method uses an excess of an insoluble solid, and evaluate what would go wrong if a soluble alkali were used instead.
questions.solution:
The method depends on two properties of the solid: that it is added in **excess**, and that it is **insoluble**. Each solves a different problem.

Adding the solid **in excess** means adding more than can possibly react. This guarantees that **all of the acid is used up**, because there is always solid left for it to react with. That matters because any **leftover acid** would remain in the solution and be crystallised along with the salt, giving an **impure** product.

Using an **insoluble** solid means the leftover can be got rid of. Because it does not dissolve, **filtration** removes it completely: it stays in the filter paper while the salt solution passes through. So the excess, which would be a contaminant in any other method, becomes something that can simply be lifted out.

If a **soluble alkali** such as sodium hydroxide solution were used instead, both advantages would be lost. First, the **endpoint would not be visible**. With an insoluble solid you can see when to stop, because the solid stops disappearing and collects at the bottom. With two colourless solutions there is nothing to see, so you would have to add exactly the right volume — which in practice means a **titration** with an indicator, a different and more elaborate experiment.

Second, and more seriously, **any excess alkali would be dissolved**. It would pass straight through the filter paper with the salt and be left behind when the water evaporated, so the crystals would be contaminated with alkali. Unlike an excess of solid, there is no simple way to remove it.

So the choice is not arbitrary. An excess of an insoluble solid converts an invisible endpoint into a visible one, and converts an unavoidable contaminant into something removable — which is why this is the standard route to a soluble salt, and why the specification specifies an **insoluble oxide or carbonate** for the required practical.

examTechnique.body:
The steps are easy to learn and the **reasons** are what is asked for. For each stage be ready to say **why**: warming is about **rate**, excess is about **using all the acid**, insolubility is about being able to **filter**, the water bath is about **even heating**, and slow evaporation is about **crystal size**.

Read the question for the words **pure** and **dry**: they are two different requirements met by two different parts of the method.
examinerErrors: Saying the solid is added in excess without saying that this uses up **all the acid**.
Omitting the second half of the reason — that the excess can be **filtered off because it is insoluble**.
Evaporating to **dryness**, which gives a powder rather than crystals.
Using a **Bunsen flame** for the evaporation instead of a **water bath**.
Confusing the two heating steps: the **acid** is warmed with a Bunsen, the **solution** is evaporated on a water bath.
Leaving out **slow evaporation**, so the answer cannot explain crystal size.
Answering only **purity** when the question asks for **pure, dry** crystals.
Giving an observation that does not match the solid used — **fizzing stops** applies to a carbonate, not an oxide.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer explains the **design**, not just the steps. It says that an insoluble solid in excess solves two problems at once — it makes the endpoint **visible** and it makes the excess **removable** — and it can say what would go wrong with a soluble alkali: no visible endpoint, and a dissolved excess that filtration cannot touch. It keeps the two heating stages apart, stops the evaporation at the **point of crystallisation** and explains crystal size in terms of the particles having **time to form a regular lattice**. And it answers **pure** and **dry** separately, because they are earned by different steps.
